newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-WOMEN COOK UP FEAST AT OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WOMEN COOK UP FEAST AT OPEN.

text.p: All the ingredients for a mouth-watering second week of women's tennis are there on the final week's menu of the Australian Open.
The shock departure of second seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario of Spain has turned up the heat for a cordon bleu final -- 21 times grand slam winner Steffi Graf against teen prodigy Martina Hingis.

The pressure is on Graf, who is unbeaten in her past six grand slam tournaments but whose form has been way short of that which carried her to a five-set victory over Hingis in the year-ending WTA championship.
The German says she is fully focussed on reaching her first Melbourne final in three years after missing the past two Opens through injury.
However, her father Peter's trial on tax evasion charges is expected to reach a verdict on January 24, just a few hours before the final.
Graf has also confirmed the professional women's tennis circuit is investigating claims she took appearance money against the tour's rules. She risks a three-month ban if the allegations are proved.
While Graf had to swallow questions about her father's trial and the appearance money allegations, it was a week of caviar and champagne for the Hingis family.
The 16-year-old, who is coached by her mother Melanie, has not dropped a set while playing what she described as "almost perfect tennis".
After crushing Austria's Barbara Schett in just 50 minutes in the third round, she said: "It was almost a practice, shorter than a practice.
"It's getting better and better, and hoepfully I'll never have a big match until the semis or whatever."
Czechoslovak-born Hingis was in the headlines in the first week for a five-year deal with an Italian sportswear label worth up to US$12 million if she reaches world number one.
Graf, who will take her career earnings over $20 million is she wins here, is playing her first tournament since beating Hingis in that epic finale to last year's tour.
The German had barely warmed up when her first round opponent retired with an injury, and had rusty starts in her next two matches before eventually finding rhythm.
Graf will next play 12th seeded South African Amanda Coetzer, a semifinalist here last year who has enjoyed a drama-free run, failing to drop a set in the tournament.
For 10th seed Brenda Schultz McCarthy, the tournament turned sour when she crashed out in the second round, becoming the only seed in the top half of the draw to miss the second week.
Graf is likely to face American seventh seed Lindsay Davenport in the quarter-finals and Spanish third seed Conchita Martinez in the semifinals.

Sanchez Vicario, attempting to win her first Australian Open final, crashed out on Saturday to unheralded Belgian Dominique van Roost in the third round to give Hingis a seemingly clear run to the final from the bottom half of the draw.
Her toughest match will probably come in the semifinal, possibly against 15th seeded American Chanda Rubin.
One unseeded player could still cook up a surprise. Former champion Mary Pierce is on her best form for two years and is definitely the crowd's favourite in the women's draw.

Melbourne tennis fans are hungry for a new heroine to replace Graf and the absent Monica Seles. Pierce would be the icing on the cake but Hingis, a brash teenager who enjoys chicken fajitas, would be just as tasty.
